gene.short: A stretch of DNA, the body's chemical instruction code inherited from both parents, that holds the recipe for one protein (or a few). You carry two copies of most genes, one from each parent.

familial-aggregation.short: When a trait clusters in families: relatives are more alike than unrelated people. Shared genes or a shared home life can cause it.

heritability.short: The share of the differences between people in one group, at one time, that goes with differences in their genes (0–100%). It describes a group, not how much of one person's trait is genetic.

trainability.short: How much a person improves (e.g. in VO2max) when given a set amount of training.

polymorphism.short: A spot in the DNA where people commonly differ, so a gene comes in two or more versions. A one-letter difference is called a SNP ('snip').

allele.short: One version of a gene at a polymorphism, e.g. R or X in the ACTN3 gene. You get one allele from each parent.

genotype.short: The pair of alleles a person carries at one polymorphism, e.g. RR, RX or XX for ACTN3.

odds-ratio.short: How much more common something is in one group than in another, as a ratio of odds. OR 1.0 means no difference; OR 1.35 means the odds are 35% higher.

gwas.short: A study that tests hundreds of thousands of polymorphisms across all the DNA at once, looking for ones linked to a trait. So many tests make chance hits likely, so findings need repeating in new people.

polygenic-score.short: One number made by adding up the 'favourable' alleles a person carries at many polymorphisms, each with a tiny effect, to estimate a trait.

direct-to-consumer-test.short: A genetic test sold straight to the public (often by post, with a saliva sample), without a doctor or genetic counsellor.

non-responder.short: Someone whose measured change after training is no bigger than the test's noise (e.g. within its typical error). A label for one result, not proof the person can't improve.

dose-response.short: How the effect changes with the amount (dose) given: here, how the training gain grows with more sessions or minutes a week.
